july_morning.label: July Morning
july_morning.intro: A Bulgarian summer ritual: stay up through the short night and greet the very first sunrise of July, ideally with your feet in the sand of the Black Sea coast.
funFacts: The tradition began in 1985 in Varna and now draws thousands to the Black Sea coast and the Danube every 1 July.
Its name comes from "July Morning", a 1971 song by the British rock band Uriah Heep.
Cape Shabla is Bulgaria's easternmost point, so the sun comes up there before anywhere else in the country.

world_ufo_day.label: World UFO Day
world_ufo_day.intro: An evening for looking up. Sky-watchers gather on 2 July, the date of the alleged 1947 crash near Roswell, to swap stories about lights that nobody can quite explain.
funFacts: The US Air Force later put the Roswell debris down to a balloon from the secret Project Mogul, which listened for Soviet nuclear tests.
Some people mark the day on 24 June instead, when pilot Kenneth Arnold's 1947 sighting gave the world the phrase "flying saucer".
Officials have largely dropped "UFO": since 2022 the term of choice in the US is UAP, unidentified anomalous phenomena.

eat_beans_day.label: Eat Beans Day
eat_beans_day.intro: A cheerful nudge towards the most underrated thing in the cupboard. Beans are cheap, filling and turn up in almost every cuisine on earth.
funFacts: Beans host rhizobia bacteria in their root nodules that pull nitrogen out of the air, leaving the soil richer than they found it.
Heinz baked beans first reached Britain in 1886 as an imported delicacy sold at Fortnum & Mason.
Raw kidney beans are mildly toxic: they contain phytohaemagglutinin and have to be boiled properly before eating.

alice_in_wonderland_day.label: Alice in Wonderland Day
alice_in_wonderland_day.intro: On this date in 1862 a boat trip near Oxford turned into one of the strangest and best-loved stories ever told. A good day for tea parties and impossible logic.
funFacts: On 4 July 1862 Lewis Carroll rowed up the Isis with the three Liddell sisters and invented the tale to pass the time.
Alice Liddell was ten years old on that trip, and it was she who asked Carroll to write the story down.
The book has never been out of print and has been translated into 174 languages.

mechanical_pencil_day.label: Mechanical Pencil Day
mechanical_pencil_day.intro: A small salute to the pencil that never needs sharpening. Click, and there is a fresh millimetre of lead waiting for you.
funFacts: The first patent for a refillable pencil with a lead-propelling mechanism went to Sampson Mordan and John Isaac Hawkins in Britain in 1822.
The oldest known example was recovered from the wreck of HMS Pandora, which sank in 1791.
Pencil lead has never contained lead: it is a mix of graphite and clay, and more clay means a harder, lighter line.

international_kissing_day.label: International Kissing Day
international_kissing_day.intro: A reminder that a kiss costs nothing and is worth a great deal. The day took shape in Britain in the 1990s and has been happily copied ever since.
funFacts: Kissing has its own field of research with a suitably serious name: philematology.
The longest kiss on record lasted more than 58 hours, set by a Thai couple in Pattaya in 2013.
Latin had three separate words for it: osculum for friendship, basium for affection and savium for passion.

world_chocolate_day.label: World Chocolate Day
world_chocolate_day.intro: One day a year when nobody has to justify the second piece. Dark, milk or white, chocolate is the closest thing the world has to a universal treat.
funFacts: Cacao beans once worked as money: the Aztecs used them to pay tribute and to buy everyday goods.
For most of its history chocolate was a drink; the first bar you could bite came from J. S. Fry & Sons in Bristol in 1847.
White chocolate contains cocoa butter but no cocoa solids, which is exactly why it never turns brown.

video_game_day.label: Video Game Day
video_game_day.intro: Controllers out. A day for the pixels of your childhood, the co-op sessions on the sofa and that one level you still have not finished.
funFacts: One of the earliest video games, "Tennis for Two", ran on an oscilloscope built by physicist William Higinbotham in 1958.
An early Pong machine reportedly stopped working because its coin box was jammed completely full of quarters.
Nintendo was founded in 1889 and spent its first decades making hanafuda playing cards.

sugar_cookie_day.label: National Sugar Cookie Day
sugar_cookie_day.intro: Butter, sugar, flour, a cookie cutter. The sugar cookie is deliberately plain so that the icing, the sprinkles and the shape can do the talking.
funFacts: The recipe is traced to German Protestant settlers in Nazareth, Pennsylvania, in the 18th century.
Pennsylvania liked it enough to make the Nazareth sugar cookie its official state cookie in 2001.
Sugar only became an everyday ingredient in Europe after Franz Karl Achard opened the first beet sugar factory in 1801.

pina_colada_day.label: National Piña Colada Day
pina_colada_day.intro: Pineapple, coconut cream, rum and a lot of ice. The piña colada tastes like a holiday even when you are drinking it on a rainy Tuesday.
funFacts: Puerto Rico made the piña colada its official national drink in 1978.
The Caribe Hilton in San Juan claims its bartender Ramón "Monchito" Marrero mixed the first one in 1954.
The name is simply Spanish for "strained pineapple".

bandoneon_day.label: Day of the Bandoneón
bandoneon_day.intro: Argentina celebrates the wheezing, sighing box that gives tango its voice. It is held between both hands and played by pushing and pulling the bellows.
funFacts: The date is the birthday of Aníbal Troilo, born on 11 July 1914 and still the most famous bandoneonist of all.
The instrument is German: it is named after the Krefeld music dealer Heinrich Band and was first meant for church and popular tunes.
Bandoneons were never mass-produced in Argentina, and German production stopped around the Second World War, so old instruments are rare and pricey.

etch_a_sketch_day.label: Etch A Sketch Day
etch_a_sketch_day.intro: Two knobs, one line, no undo button. The red drawing toy has been frustrating and delighting people in equal measure since this date in 1960.
funFacts: It went on sale on 12 July 1960 for $2.99 and has since sold more than 100 million units worldwide.
It was invented in France by the electrician André Cassagnes and manufactured by the Ohio Art Company in the US.
The screen is coated on the inside with aluminium powder; the stylus scrapes it away and a good shake puts it back.

embrace_your_geekness_day.label: Embrace Your Geekness Day
embrace_your_geekness_day.intro: Permission, officially granted, to be enthusiastic in public about the thing you know far too much about. Comics, trains, spreadsheets, dinosaurs: all welcome.
funFacts: "Geek" started out as a fairground word for a sideshow performer before it came to mean a devoted specialist.
"Nerd" first appeared in print in Dr. Seuss's 1950 picture book "If I Ran the Zoo".
The first San Diego Comic-Con in 1970 drew a few hundred visitors; today it fills the city with well over 100,000.

world_chimpanzee_day.label: World Chimpanzee Day
world_chimpanzee_day.intro: A day for our closest living relatives, marking the date Jane Goodall first walked into the forest at Gombe and started watching chimpanzees properly.
funFacts: Goodall arrived at Gombe Stream in Tanzania on 14 July 1960; the day has been celebrated since 2018.
She watched chimps strip leaves off twigs to fish termites out of a mound, the first record of a non-human animal making a tool.
Chimpanzees share roughly 99 percent of their DNA with us and greet each other with hugs, kisses and back pats.

tapioca_pudding_day.label: National Tapioca Pudding Day
tapioca_pudding_day.intro: Small translucent pearls that go delightfully chewy when cooked. Tapioca has been comfort food for generations and, more recently, the best part of bubble tea.
funFacts: Tapioca is pure starch washed out of the cassava root, a staple crop for hundreds of millions of people in the tropics.
Raw cassava is toxic and has to be processed first; the washed-out starch itself is perfectly harmless.
The chewy black pearls in bubble tea are tapioca too, a Taiwanese invention from the 1980s.

world_snake_day.label: World Snake Day
world_snake_day.intro: A day for the most misunderstood animals in the garden. Snakes have no legs, no eyelids and no ears, and still manage to live almost everywhere on earth.
funFacts: There are more than 3,000 snake species; only about 200 of them are considered dangerous to humans.
Snakes cannot blink: a clear scale called the brille covers each eye and is shed along with the skin.
They smell with their tongue, which carries scent particles to the Jacobson's organ in the roof of the mouth.

world_emoji_day.label: World Emoji Day
world_emoji_day.intro: The day the little yellow faces get their own party. Look at the calendar emoji on your phone and you will see exactly why 17 July was chosen.
funFacts: The date comes from the calendar emoji, which shows 17 July on Apple devices — the day iCal was announced in 2002.
World Emoji Day was launched in 2014 by Jeremy Burge, the founder of Emojipedia.
In 2015 Oxford Dictionaries picked the "face with tears of joy" as word of the year, the first time a pictograph won.

world_listening_day.label: World Listening Day
world_listening_day.intro: An invitation to stop talking for a moment and pay attention to how the world actually sounds — the birds, the traffic, the hum of your own kitchen.
funFacts: The date is the birthday of Canadian composer R. Murray Schafer, born on 18 July 1933, who popularised the idea of the soundscape.
The World Listening Project started the day in 2010; people mark it with listening walks and field recordings.
In the world's quietest rooms, anechoic chambers, sound levels drop below zero decibels and you can hear your own blood.

palace_day.label: Palace Day
palace_day.intro: Europe's royal residences open their archives and their side doors online, sharing the stories, staircases and quirks that visitors usually walk straight past.
funFacts: The Network of European Royal Residences launched #PalaceDay in 2016; every year has a different theme.
The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles is about 73 metres long and lined with 357 mirrors.
Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna has 1,441 rooms, of which only around 40 are open to visitors.

international_chess_day.label: International Chess Day
international_chess_day.intro: Sixty-four squares, thirty-two pieces and more possible games than there are atoms in the observable universe. Time to challenge someone.
funFacts: The date marks the founding of the world chess federation FIDE in Paris on 20 July 1924; the UN recognised the day in 2019.
After only four moves each, more than 288 billion different positions are possible.
Chess grew out of the Indian game chaturanga, played from around the 6th century onwards.

junk_food_day.label: National Junk Food Day
junk_food_day.intro: One day off from the good intentions. Burgers, crisps, gummy sweets — whatever it is you pretend not to eat, today it goes on the plate without comment.
funFacts: The term "junk food" was popularised in the 1970s, notably by nutrition campaigner Michael Jacobson in 1972.
Legend has it the potato crisp was born in Saratoga Springs in 1853, when a cook sliced potatoes wafer-thin for a fussy guest.
US surveys found that on any given day about a third of adults eat fast food.

hammock_day.label: National Hammock Day
hammock_day.intro: The world's most persuasive argument for doing nothing. Two trees, a length of cloth, and the afternoon takes care of itself.
funFacts: The word travelled into English via the Spanish hamaca from the Taíno language of the Caribbean.
Sailors slept in hammocks below deck for centuries because they swing with the roll of the ship instead of against it.
From Apollo 12 onwards, astronauts slept in hammocks strung inside the lunar module.

vanilla_ice_cream_day.label: National Vanilla Ice Cream Day
vanilla_ice_cream_day.intro: The flavour everyone calls plain and everyone keeps ordering. Real vanilla ice cream is anything but boring — it starts with the pod of an orchid.
funFacts: Vanilla comes from an orchid, and outside its Mexican home every flower has to be pollinated by hand.
The hand-pollination trick was worked out in 1841 by Edmond Albius, a twelve-year-old on the island of Réunion.
Thomas Jefferson's handwritten vanilla ice cream recipe is kept in the Library of Congress.

tequila_day.label: National Tequila Day
tequila_day.intro: A toast to the spirit of the blue agave. Sipped slowly rather than knocked back, good tequila tastes of pepper, earth and roasted plant hearts.
funFacts: Tequila may only be made from blue agave and only in defined regions of Mexico, above all the state of Jalisco.
The agave landscape around the town of Tequila has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2006.
An agave grows for six to ten years before its heart, the piña, is cut out; it often weighs more than 40 kilograms.

carousel_day.label: National Merry-Go-Round Day
carousel_day.intro: Painted horses, a brass pole and an organ playing slightly out of tune. The carousel is the one fairground ride that works just as well at three as at eighty-three.
funFacts: On 25 July 1871 William Schneider of Davenport, Iowa was granted the first American carousel patent.
The name comes from the Italian carosello, a horseback game that knights used as riding practice.
European carousels usually turn clockwise, American ones the other way, so riders can grab the brass ring with the right hand.

esperanto_day.label: Esperanto Day
esperanto_day.intro: The birthday of a language built on purpose to be easy and neutral. Speakers around the world mark the day the very first Esperanto textbook appeared.
funFacts: On 26 July 1887 L. L. Zamenhof published the Unua Libro, the first textbook of the language.
He signed it "Doktoro Esperanto", meaning "one who hopes" — and the pseudonym became the name of the language.
Esperanto has sixteen grammatical rules, no irregular verbs, and a small number of native speakers who grew up with it at home.

sleepy_head_day.label: National Sleepy Head Day
sleepy_head_day.intro: Finland's revenge on late risers. Whoever is still in bed gets woken with water — and in one town a well-known guest ends up in the sea before breakfast.
funFacts: In Naantali a Finnish celebrity is thrown into the harbour at 7 a.m.; who it will be is kept secret until the moment itself.
The custom goes back to the Middle Ages, when the last sleeper in the house was thought to be lazy for the rest of the year.
Every mayor of Naantali has taken the plunge at least once.

singing_telegram_day.label: Singing Telegram Day
singing_telegram_day.intro: The day a telegram learned to sing. Instead of the usual bad news, a Western Union operator delivered a birthday greeting down the telephone — in tune.
funFacts: On 28 July 1933 operator Lucille Lipps sang a birthday message to the singer Rudy Vallée, the first singing telegram.
It was the idea of PR man George P. Oslin, who was told he was making a laughing stock of the company.
Western Union finally shut down its telegram service in 2006, after more than 150 years.

chicken_wing_day.label: National Chicken Wing Day
chicken_wing_day.intro: Sticky fingers, a pile of napkins and a bowl of blue cheese dip. The chicken wing went from kitchen scrap to bar-food royalty in a single generation.
funFacts: In 1977 the city of Buffalo declared 29 July Chicken Wing Day, honouring Anchor Bar co-owner Frank Bellissimo.
Buffalo wings are said to have been invented at that bar in 1964; before then wings mostly ended up in the stockpot.
Buffalo, New York holds an annual wing festival whose hall of fame is called the Hall of Flame.

paperback_book_day.label: Paperback Book Day
paperback_book_day.intro: The day good books stopped being expensive. Ten cheap little volumes went on sale in 1935 and changed who was allowed to own a library.
funFacts: On 30 July 1935 Penguin published its first ten paperbacks at sixpence each — the price of a packet of cigarettes.
Allen Lane had the idea after finding nothing worth reading at a railway station bookstall; Woolworths took the first big order.
The covers were colour-coded: orange for fiction, green for crime, dark blue for biography.

raspberry_cake_day.label: National Raspberry Cake Day
raspberry_cake_day.intro: The last day of July, and raspberry season is at its peak. Fold them into a sponge, pile them on cream, or simply eat them off your fingertips.
funFacts: Botanically a raspberry is not a berry at all but an aggregate fruit made of dozens of tiny drupelets.
Raspberries come off their core when picked, which is why they are hollow; blackberries keep theirs.
They belong to the rose family, along with apples, pears, cherries and strawberries.
